GitHub’s new Git storage architecture is built so thousands of agents can push to a single repository at once. Here’s how it works.

Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running.

Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post, we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage.

We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.

The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components.

We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes:

Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes.

We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then.

We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to:

On top of that, the system had to be able to improve overall reliability and scale globally.

In May of 2026, hot on the heels of the initial Azure migration, we started working on a design that could meet those demands. We tried several approaches. In all of them, pack data lived in Azure Blob Storage, and in some we experimented with keeping reference state there too. We’ll cover some of the trade-offs we found below, but we settled on a design we felt maximized throughput while preserving the correctness, durability, availability, and latency guarantees a platform like GitHub requires. We called it “Rubicon,” a nod to the point of no return the industry crossed with agentic development.

Let’s walk through Rubicon from the top down. Many things stay the same: requests from Git clients, the API, and the web UI arrive at Spokes, which still handles routing and load balancing, and serves the internal API that the rest of GitHub uses to read and write repository data. Spokes also maintains its role as a placement and balancing service, maintaining the partitioning, isolation, and tenant fairness required for horizontal scale. The data plane underneath Spokes, in contrast, is new.

Spokes routes each request to one of a small group of virtual replicas assigned to that repository. Virtual replicas are a single fleet of disposable compute that serves reads, writes, or both. A virtual replica’s local disk is a cache that can be rebuilt at any time.

Spokes routes a repository’s traffic to the same virtual replicas when it can, which keeps their caches warm and latency low, but nothing about correctness depends on a request landing on any particular virtual replica. When a virtual replica goes away, the repository’s other virtual replicas keep serving, and a replacement fills its cache as traffic arrives.

When a repository gets busy, we add more virtual replicas. Separately, a fleet of compaction nodes works in the background, directly against Blob Storage and Ref-CAS, to merge each repository’s packs and remove unreachable objects. That work never runs on a virtual replica, meaning their CPU and memory can be almost entirely dedicated to serving requests.

Let’s walk the architecture from the perspective of a write and a read:

There are many distinct approaches we’ve taken within the new architecture, from the software stack on the virtual replicas to how traffic routing and workload scheduling are tuned for different use cases (e.g., many small repos vs. one large one). Let’s dive deep into two components of the architecture and tell their stories centered on the two design principles.

Object storage services like Azure Blob Storage are incredibly good at what they do, and natural fits for many data-heavy applications like source code storage. They are durable and replicated, hold as much as we need them to, have a relatively low cost per byte, and deliver exceptionally high aggregate throughput so long as traffic is spread across many keys. As a result, nearly everything durable in the new Git storage architecture lives in Azure Blob Storage, including:

Most of that data is written once to a distinct key and never changes afterward, which is what makes it highly suitable for Blob Storage.

References are the opposite. A busy repository’s references are a relatively small piece of state that many writes race to update at the same time. That access pattern is harder to serve from Blob Storage, and our first prototypes showed us why. Object storage for this kind of workload is an intuitive choice, and one that works well up to a certain level of scale: conditional writes give a compare-and-swap for free, and the data is already durable and replicated. However, we ran into a difficult set of choices, illustrated below by two approaches we tried.

Our first approach was a write-ahead log for all of a repository’s references, indexed by a single blob. Every update is a conditional write against that blob. It’s correct, and reads are cheap: a virtual replica asks whether the blob has changed, and if it hasn’t, it’s done. Writes are where it falls short. Only one conditional write to a blob can be in flight at a time, so even when we batch every push that arrives during a write into the next one, the repository’s write ceiling is one write per round trip to a single blob. In practice, this netted us write throughput in the mid-hundreds per second.

Our second approach split the references across several segment blobs, with each reference hashing to one of them. Writes to references in different segments no longer wait on each other, which raises the ceiling. But a read now has to check every segment to know whether anything changed, and it’s only as fast as the slowest segment. We’d traded write latency for read latency, and reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude. We can visualize this by showing multiple writes and a read side by side:

Neither option met every requirement, so we built something else: a replicated log service dedicated to references, or the Ref-CAS service. This is the (small) consensus group we said at the end of the last post was still somewhere in the stack. Here’s how it works.

Each reference update in Ref-CAS is a compare-and-swap committed by a quorum. A transaction locks only the references it touches, checks that each one still has the value the writer expects, and becomes visible once a majority of the log’s replicas have recorded it. Agents mostly push to their own branches, so most updates don’t contend, and they replicate in parallel. When two pushes do update the same reference, only one will append to the log.

Each commit to Ref-CAS gets a log sequence number (LSN), and the repository’s version is the LSN of its latest commit. Reads start with a version check against that version. A virtual replica sends the version of the reference state it already holds. If that version is still current, the reply carries no references at all, and an unchanged repository costs a single comparison. If the virtual replica is behind, it gets back the current references and version, along with pointers to pack data and anything else that needs to be known, such as when the last garbage collection cycle occurred.

Unlike the consensus group in our legacy architecture, Ref-CAS never holds or validates object data. It only stores pointers to it. A virtual replica uploads a push’s pack to Blob Storage before it commits the reference transaction. A reference only ever points at objects that are already durable.

These approaches allow us to transact reference state alone in the tens of thousands of operations per second, and provide a baseline for additional annotations on the replication log that help reads decide what to download for a given request.

But supporting thousands of writes per second on a single repository creates a second-order problem: maintaining the performance of reads and writes. For that, we needed a different approach to compaction.

Every push adds a pack to Blob Storage. Git can serve a repository from many packs, but each additional pack makes lookups slightly more expensive, so the pack count can’t grow without bound. In our legacy architecture, compaction runs on the same replicas that serve traffic, and it has to run on every replica. In the new architecture, it runs entirely in the background on separate nodes, directly against durable storage, using the Ref-CAS service to notify virtual replicas of the evolving state.

Compaction nodes each claim ownership over a subset of the repository’s data via a lease, which allows us to scale compaction horizontally. Here’s how one compaction node works through a single shard of a repository’s packs:

The node first takes a lease on the shard in Blob Storage, so only one node compacts a shard at a time. Meanwhile, virtual replicas keep uploading packs and listing them in the pack manifest. The node reads the manifest to find new packs and collects them into an open segment, which is effectively a holding ground for data about to be compacted. When the segment reaches a defined limit based on pack count, size, or age, it seals the segment so it accepts no new packs, then combines its packs into fewer, larger ones. While compaction happens, the next segment for the shard can begin capturing its input packs. Before anything is published, the node checks that the new packs contain exactly the same objects as the inputs. It then uploads the new packs and adds them to the manifest. A second transaction removes the inputs from the manifest, and cleanup deletes them later.

To scale out, this process runs independently for many shards at once. Each pack’s hash maps to a shard, so adding shards and nodes adds compaction throughput. A compacted pack that’s still under the size limit goes back into a shard by its own hash and merges again, so packs grow in tiers until they reach the limit. The net result is an effectively flat pack count while pushes climb:

Compaction merges packs, but it keeps every object. Garbage collection is the step that removes objects nothing references anymore, like the ones left behind by deleted branches and force-pushes. In our new architecture, garbage collection works very similarly to compaction by using dedicated workers to handle the compute-heavy portion. It also has a few special behaviors for safely removing data, which are worthy of their own discussion.

Using these approaches, we’ve been able to consistently demonstrate a flat latency curve as writes climb, and we have other planned optimizations to make the compaction and garbage collection processes themselves more performant.

The two principles we started with let each part of this architecture scale on its own. We scale reads and writes by adding virtual replicas. Ref-CAS orders each reference independently instead of the whole repository. We scale maintenance by adding compaction nodes. Our goal is for every repository, from one developer’s side project to the busiest monorepo, to run on the same architecture with no special handling for the busy ones. Repositories don’t stay small. A side project can pick up a fleet of agents overnight, and it shouldn’t need a migration or special handling from us to keep up. One architecture also means every improvement we make reaches every repository at once.

This foundation lets us do a lot more. We’re focused on three areas next: scaling the architecture beyond what we can predict we’ll need today, making agents more efficient at the work they do on GitHub, and evolving Git itself for agentic development.

We have plans to take this architecture further. Each of these improvements lets a repository handle more activity while reducing the work behind each request:

Scaling the infrastructure is one side of supporting agents. The other side is making each agent operation cheaper: fewer bytes to fetch, fewer round trips, and less waiting on changes. Each of these fast-follow items builds on the storage work in this post:

We also have work to do in Git itself. GitHub has been a longtime contributor to the Git project, and we’re not stopping now. A few examples of the work we’re excited to continue:

Agents have changed how software gets built. GitHub and Git are changing with it. We’re excited to take this new architecture across the starting line. It’s available in a limited private preview now, with a broader rollout early next year. We can’t wait to see what teams build when the number of agents working on a repository is limited by their ideas. We’ll keep evolving Git and GitHub alongside our customers and the Git community.

Brian is a Principal Software Engineer working on the storage and core services that power all repository interactions on GitHub.

#10056. GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

The reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

In the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that new capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every new request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

The discipline is new enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this issue.

Good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

That's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

Writing code got faster. The work around it didn’t. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment.

This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan.

What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable plan, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped issues, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.

After spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.

That review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.

Smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.

Your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard shows intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.

Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.

Figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up issues, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next plan starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.

Take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?

You don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count says you are.

We covered this topic live at GitHub Universe 2026 in “Agentic Engineering: Past the Pilot.”

#10053. Persistent incrementality in Rust

There is this cool idea: incremental computations. The concept is simple, if you calculated something and then inputs change, it doesn't have to mean that you need to recompute everything. Most of your computations might still be valid, and quite often it is the case that you only need to redo a small chunk of changes.

This concept usually works the best when you need to compute a lot of stuff, and there are a lot of inputs, and these inputs change independently with different degree of likelihood. Probably, the most common example is incremental compilation, which makes the compilation reuse as much work as possible, making iterations during development much faster. The interesting part is "iterating": note that incremental compilation doesn't necessarily makes cold builds faster. The compiler performance might be roughly the same with and without incrementality, it's just repeated reuse of compiler artifacts becomes more efficient. Most likely you've heard of it. And if you did, you probably know that incremental compilation is not easy (1, 2, 3). But it's cool!

And if incremental computations concept applies well to compilers, it applies even better to LSP servers, because user makes edits in the editor much more often than they recompile code, and each keystroke must change the editor state in milliseconds (unless you go full vibe and don't need an IDE anymore, that is).

It could be somewhat related to the fact that rust-analyzer uses salsa as the central part of its architecture. Salsa is a library that makes incremental computations very convenient and efficient. There is one drawback, though. It is mainly designed to work in memory. And we'll touch on how it works in a bit.

For project like Rust Glancer that tries to keep the memory usage as low as possible, this doesn't work. Because of that, for a long time Rust Glancer didn't use incremental computations, and instead had a sophisticated network of persistent caches with sharding and targeted optimizations to make computations efficient. And it worked, for a while. But this approach doesn't scale very well: if you need to maintain a manually implemented custom cache format, optimize it, and tie computations to it, then the more efficiency you seek, the more complexity you get. Basically, the complexity is "quadratic": it grows as O(computations_complexity * cache_implementation_complexity) because both are interconnected (sorry, CS purists, for this crime).

So... Rust Glancer got to a point where it would really benefit from persistent incremental computations. And the search for it turned out to be really interesting, so in this blog post we'll be discussing how incremental computations can work in memory and how to make this approach work with persistency.

Before we start discussing how incremental computations work under the hood, let's see how it looks like.

If you know how to use Salsa feel free to jump to the next section. If you're familiar with red-green algorithm and in-memory approach that Salsa uses, you can skip to where persistency starts.

Now, incremental computations are somewhat tricky to explain in a blog post, because the value of it requires an application to be somewhat big. So we will need an example that is big enough to show the value of incrementality, but small enough to discuss here. It's a bit absurd, but I hope you can focus on the idea, not on the value of the snippet at hand.

Let's imagine that we're doing a weird text processor that would count the words in all the files in the directory, and decide whether this count is funny. And to make things more interesting, the files can include other files.

How would that look if implemented naively? Something like that, most likely (well, let's ignore the IO):

Now, let's try Salsa. It should let us make some computations reusable. Here's how it would look like:

The code looks pretty similar! However, let's inspect the output.

The first call matches the naive example:

Note: not only we did not call word_count(a), we did not call is_haha_number as well!

Salsa can see that file b changed, and it re-run word_count for it. But the output did not change, so all the previous computations are valid: nothing to be run.

The word count in b changed, and a includes b, so we need to re-run all three queries. But the order is inversed! This is because we have a dependency graph internally, and we're walking through the dependency tree and re-execute changed queries from the "leaves" to the "root".

We have changed b from 65 to 67 words, so a now has 69 words. Result is still true, but we did have to update the computations. If we would've had another query that depended on is_haha_number, that's where validation would've stopped and all the queries above wouldn't need to run.

We have changed dependencies of a, so there is no b anymore. So we start with what we know: word_count for a. It now has a not-yet-tracked dependency on c, so we go to c after a. And the rest is the same.

So I hope you get the idea now: each query result is memorized, and if we discover that the output of this query did not change, we don't need to recompute the queries that depend on this input. Or rather, if all the queries that query X depends on did not change, then query X does not need to be recomputed.

And now imagine that you have 700 dependencies in your workspace. A single file changed in the topmost dependency. 699 dependencies can keep their result! Within a single crate, still only one file has changed, so the information about all the other files at least partially stays the same. We only need to redo the computations that actually matter.

And most importantly, we don't need to write any of this tracking code ourselves, Salsa gives it to us for free.

Well, it's really not trivial. If you want to have a more formal deep dive, I suggest the following reads:

Imagine that each query, combined with its arguments, is an object. This object can have a bunch of metadata, stating whether it was already computed, when it happened, what was the output, and what's the object dependencies. Let's call this metadata a "memo".

Side note: why is "combined with its arguments?" important? Because we cannot memoize is_haha_number, but we can memoize is_haha_number(420), so you can think of it as a mapping of (function, arguments) -> output

And imagine that you have inputs: something that user provides, and this something can be explicitly requested by a query.

We might also say that the database has a revision, initially 1. When you change some input, the revision gets bumped to 2, and so on. This revision can be used as "when it happened" (or rather, "when it change last time") inside of the memo.

Now, we've provided our inputs and invoke a query. It has some associated code that can internally do two things:

If query requests an input, it should record that it depends on this input. So if input changes, it must be recomputed.

If query requests another query, we might check if the corresponding query has a memo with a computed value. If it has, we need to make sure that it is valid for the revision we're at. If it is: great! It can be reused, and we don't need to recompute it. Otherwise, we need to recursively go into this query. Obviously, we also record a dependency on this query.

During the execution, we'll collect all the inputs and all the dependency queries, and ultimately we'll finally compute the result of our query. And when we do, we can fill out the memo: record the revision and the output.

And... done! Next time you request an output, we will look at this query object memo. If inputs did not change, we can just hand out the result. If they changed, we go down the query line, and do the same thing. So naturally only the things that actually might have changed will be recomputed.

Oh, but there is one more important detail here, that makes everything even better. If revision changed, it does not automatically mean that we need to recompute this query. We might recompute dependencies, and compare them to the old values. If all the outputs are the equal to the old ones (imagine that word_count(a) changed from 67 to 69, but is_haha_number still returns true true: the query that depends on is_haha_number might not get invalidated), we can just mark the current version as verified and return the old result. And it can matter a lot when the expensive query has a lot of cheap dependencies.

Obviously, it's an overly simplified explanation. In practice, there are many, many caveats, tricky parts, and optimizations that make the experience work well. But my job here is to give you an idea; if you've become interested in the topic, I'd recommend looking to Salsa source code, it's very interesting.

And Salsa is awesome! With one caveat. It works in memory only. Well, there is ongoing work on persistency there, but AFAIU it is mostly focused on storing the computations on filesystem so that they can be reloaded later (snapshot-like). It is very valuable, but we still have to store stuff in the memory. For the project like Rust Glancer we want to offload stuff to occupy less RAM.

And in practice, there are several projects that do implement various kinds of persistence:

So there are solutions for this problem, but none of them seem to be "Salsa but everything is on the filesystem".

I guess then it would be fine to build one?

As you probably guessed, I did build one. And I called it Ajika. And I'm very proud of myself for coming up with this name, yes.

The library is here, it uses stable Rust, and is generally a complete project (but I'm working on improvements!). The post, however, is not meant to promote it; obviously it's a very young library, and while so far it works really well for me, probably sticking to Salsa if it works for you is a safe choice. Not gonna sell it, do your own research :)

What I want to share is how Ajika works under the hood and what makes it different from Salsa.

But (spoiler) in general it's just two things:

And we'll get to it and see how it works, but to make everything clear, we'll need to start from something very basic.

Here's the same program we had for Salsa, but migrated to Ajika:

It looks pretty similar, with API changes mostly being a taste difference, and on a first run it has the same output.

However, the key part here is that we can add the following to the end:

And print_result will just print False. Nothing will be executed after restart! Persistency in action!

On a serious note, the main difference is the focus. When you start working on a project like that, choosing your priority can influence the design a lot. And the choice made here is being persistent-first. While Ajika provides an in-memory backend, it's mostly meant for tests. The intended use case is to use your disk.

And it starts with a very basic question that in-memory database does not have: what happens if I restart the application?

If you already have a cache locally, many things can make this cache invalid:

And similarly, given that we cache computations, it's basically an optimization. If cache gets corrupted or removed while the application is running, user would most likely prefer the cache to be discarded and computations to be repeated one more time, rather than the app crashing with "cache is not available, what do I do???".

As a result, the cache must be throw-away. Both Ajika and application supply schema versions to identify the revision, and if the stored cache doesn't match it, we reset it. If cache gets corrupted, Ajika will attempt recovery over hard failing, even if it means re-computing data from scratch.

The next most noticeable change is that most operations are fallible. Since IO is the basic property for us, and IO can fail, we need to think about it. Failed operation does not mean that cache is corrupted, but it does mean that the current query might not be computed. Typically, it can be retried, though.

Finally, the persistence is, unfortunately, a leaky abstraction. You cannot really hide from the fact that the data is outside of memory, because everything you persist must be serializable. And your interim query data might be reusable but not serializable (imagine an AST that borrows the source text: making it own the data likely will be worse), so some of the queries might be transient: we compute them once and retain while the current operation runs, but drop instead of persisting once operation ends.

Together, these properties start working rather nicely, however: your application has to be aware of persistence, but not in an annoying way. If something fails, you know about it, but you don't have to worry, since Ajika will repair things for you. If something is not serializable and it doesn't matter, it can be turned into a transient query. If you don't want your tests to rely on persistence, you just plug a memory backend in.

So let's take a look at how it works under the hood.

LLM usage disclaimer: The library discussed here is developed with use of LLMs, same as Rust Glancer. Hopefully, from this post it is evident that I'm using LLMs as a tool and have full control. It's not vibe coded.

There are three parts to Ajika: ajika itself, ajika_macros, and ajika_storage.

We'll take a look at ajika and then at ajika_storage. Macros are left as an exercise to a reader, but they're generally pretty straightforward.

Ajika itself is very easy, just check out this diagram:

...just kidding. But we'll fix that very quickly.

Still, I think it might be useful to skim through the high level details.

Side note: Ajika has its own book which does a much deeper dive on many concepts than this blog post. I'll be referring to it in some places. The con is that, unlike this handwritten blog post, the text there is mostly LLM-generated, and even if I did a lot of polishing, it shows. Eventually I'll do a full manual rewrite, but for now I figured that human-filtered-llm-guide is better than no guide at all.

Database is an entrypoint. You choose either an in-memory or persistent backend, supply Inputs and then run your operation.

Queries are the actual logic we want to execute. They are defined via ajika::query macro and in general pretty straightforward. More details on queries themselves are in the book, and we'll look at how queries are executed and what this Db object is a bit later in this post.

Inputs are somewhat more interesting. Your input type is defined through the ajika::input procedural macro, which would do some wrapping for you. And your input structure is basically a mapping: you specify a key, for example, String, and then you can use database to get an input value (or lack thereof) for whatever key you have, be it "foo" or even "bar". If you have a singleton value, like a config, you can use () as a key. Again, more on inputs can be found in the book, also might check out lazy inputs.

Outputs are probably the first part of the system that gets interesting because of persistence.

The outputs need to be stored on the filesystem, so they need to be serializable. For outputs that you don't want to serialize, you can use transient queries which will keep the value in memory only for the duration of a single operation. But even then, there is a problem: how big of an output do you want?

If you will have a 1000 very granular queries, it will mean that we need a lot of filesystem roundtrips. If you will have just a bunch of queries that compute a ton of data, you will need to deserialize a big value just to look at the part of it.

Thus, outputs offer a solution that lies in between: you can choose to return a value directly, or return a handle to this value. If you return a handle, query can use this handle to retrieve the value from the database on demand. Directly returned values are fully deserialized. This offers you a nice granularity option: you have a query that encapsulates a meaningful unit of work, but it returns you an object that contains handles for particular results. Handle is cheap to obtain and deserialize, and you only query the data you actually need. Doing is most convenient through an ajika::output macro.

As usual, more details on how to use outputs are in the book.

And now we're getting to the interesting stuff.

To perform a single run we need three things:

And there are two related concepts that make things work:

Record contains information like values metadata for a query and dependencies for it (note: values are stored separately!). Thus, Memos are released on the end of the run and then later can be reconstructed from Record on demand.

And this is an important bit: released memos don't occupy RAM. This is the key part of Ajika! During the query execution, the values can be loaded, but if you don't run any operations, you don't have to pay for it. Outputs will just wait for you inside of the filesystem! Moreover, whenever we run queries, we only load what we need, not everything.

Each time a query logic actually runs (either from run or from another query), a new Db with a new Frame is created, sharing the same Operation.

When you ask Db to execute a query, here's a typical (overly simplified) workflow:

And if during execution query receives another query result, it records it in its own Frame for reuse.

Obviously, there is a lot of bookkeeping, support for parallelism, and other things that make it complex, but in general the algorithm is pretty straightforward.

Once the operation finishes, we need to actually apply the changes. run works as a transaction, so everything that was done inside is immediately visible, but after run depending on whether run failed or succeeded, the results will either be discarded or persisted.

Checkpoint write is generally pretty straightforward:

So checkpoint on the Ajika level is pretty straightforward. What is more interesting is how Ajika storage works in general.

It's probably the most interesting part of Ajika. How do we store data in a way that is efficient?

The first version of Ajika used redb for everything. It worked, but it did not work very well. Since we don't really have a "database" per se, and more of a storage for many blobs, redb added too much overhead. However, it provides much needed features like transactions.

So, Ajika uses redb as a metadata storage: it's an index which mostly contains pointers to the values.

The values are written in "pack files": basically, just binary files to which we can append new entries. And inside of redb we can just store a pointer: (file name, offset). Each stored entry has a header with information such as length and compression algorithm. For efficiency, if the value is very small, we can keep it inline inside of redb instead of writing it to a file.

If you want to access a value, you will go to redb, check the corresponding key, and then either read it inline or read the specified pack at the specified access. Pretty simple.

Obviously, there is some more data stored there (we'll talk about identities soon, briefly), but in general it's a pretty "stupid" (hopefully in a good way) format of data storage.

However, there is one caveat: if we do it naively, the storage can grow without limits. Packs can end up with very low utilization factor, consisting mostly of "dead" values, and some of them might not be observable at all. So the storage supports maintenance: whenever you do an operation, Ajika might do a sweep that would re-pack values and update pointers, and at the end of operation Ajika will try to signal to the storage which values can be removed now. There are a few knobs you can tune here: you can specify the retention limit time (so that the very old and unused queries are cleaned up) or target storage size (which acts as a soft limit, and will affect the cleanup policy).

But ultimately, this design makes value storing and retrieval pretty efficient, and it integrates with the overall Ajika design very well.

OK, we're almost done, I promise! The last small bit: interning.

Interning values is an optimization that gives you a way to turn any object into an ID. Imagine that you have file paths. They can work as IDs, but it would probably be more efficient if you used FileId(0) / FileId(1) instead. Not only in terms of performance, but often also in terms of memory: you'd rather not have a ton of strings in memory if you don't really need them. Sometimes, interning strings on its own can be a very useful memory optimization, which is why crates like string_cache exist.

But for us, having IDs for objects can be valuable in general, because your computations results might often be linked to some other objects, and it's useful to be able to use IDs for that.

Salsa supports interning for that purpose, and Ajika does it too. However, there is one caveat for Ajika: what happens if we have our IDs allocated, they become a part of the cache, and then we restart the application?

To avoid this problem, IDs in Ajika are persisted in addition to being stored in memory, and on restart this interner state is reloaded.

Ajika development itself was an experiment: I did not create it in vacuum, I was actually porting Rust Glancer to it at the same time. And the experiment was very successful. I was able to remove a lot of complexity from Rust Glancer, and Ajika unblocked many optimizations that were not realistic with hand-rolled caches (starting with lazy body evaluation).

At the end of the experiment, Rust Glancer got performance comparable to rust-analyzer (sometimes even better!). Ajika is obviously slower than salsa, but inside of IDE the difference between 1 and 30ms is negligible, both feel instant. What matters is the low RAM usage: Rust Glancer still stays well under 100MB RAM idle on pretty big projects.

Remark: exact comparison between two will be posted in the release notes for Rust Glancer 0.5.0, so stay tuned.

As the experiments go, the branch of Rust Glancer where all of that happened is in a half-assembled state, and it's way too rushed and "prototyped" to just merge it, so I'm doing a clean reimplementation using extracted (and published) version of Ajika. It will take a while, but I'm very excited: Rust Glancer without compromises that feels instant and does not eat memory.

Thanks for reading, it turned out to be a long post. A lot of effort went into it, so I hope that it was useful, at least somewhat.

My next goal is to prepare an Ajika-based release of Rust Glancer, and after that I have a lot of ideas on how to make Ajika even faster/better/stronger. Who knows, maybe it will eventually grow into a product of its own, not merely a part of Rust Glancer ecosystem.

As usual, the best way to support if you like the project is to check out Rust Glancer, star Ajika (but only if you like it!) and/or follow me on twitter.

#10052. Baseten on Hugging Face Inference Providers 🔥

We're thrilled to share that Baseten is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!

Baseten joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub's model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Baseten is an AI infrastructure platform that covers serverless AI, training and more. With a catalog of many frontier models, Baseten makes it easy for developers to integrate a wide range of AI capabilities into their applications with minimal setup.

Baseten supports a broad spectrum of model types - from LLMs to text-to-speech and more. As part of this initial integration, Baseten is launching support for conversational and text-generation tasks on Hugging Face, enabling access to popular open-weight LLMs such as Kimi K3, latest DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM-5.2, and many more. Support for additional tasks will roll out soon!

See the full list of models supported by Baseten here.

Follow Baseten on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/baseten.

Baseten is available through the Hugging Face SDKs - huggingface_hub (>= 1.26.1) for Python and @huggingface/inference for JavaScript.

The following examples show how to use the latest DeepSeek V4 Flash through Baseten. Use a Hugging Face token to authenticate - the request will be routed to Baseten automatically.

Hugging Face Inference Providers are integrated in most Agent Harnesses - including Pi, OpenCode, Hermes Agents, OpenClaw, and more. This means you can plug baseten-hosted models straight into your favorite tools without any extra glue code. Browse the full list of integrations here.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a baseten API key you're billed on your baseten account.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us; we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.)

Important Note ‼️ PRO users get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free users, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

We would love to get your feedback! Share your thoughts and/or comments here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/HuggingDiscussions/discussions/49

Git is releasing updates addressing six security vulnerabilities affecting clones, reference handling, merges, binary patches, and imports. Here is what users need to know.

Editor’s note (November 17, 2026): This post has been updated with additional CVE information and updated guidance for GitHub Enterprise Server users. Please see the release information below for the versions that include the fixes.

Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.An attacker-controlled Git server can exploit this discrepancy to replace a clone’s .git file or directory, redirecting Git to attacker-controlled configuration or hooks.For recursive clones, this can execute attacker-controlled code during the clone. For non-recursive clones, an attacker can replace the top-level .git directory with a file pointing to attacker-controlled repository metadata. The clone can then report an error and recommend running git status in the resulting directory; following that advice can execute attacker-controlled code.The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Robert Chen reported CVE-2026-111760, which was fixed by Elijah Newren and Toon Claes, with help from Johannes Schindelin and Jeff King. Luke Martin reported CVE-2026-113408, which was fixed by Toon Claes.

pwn2addr reported CVE-2026-114466, CVE-2026-114467, and CVE-2026-114469, which were fixed by Karthik Nayak. Kaartic Sivaraam implemented the fix for CVE-2026-105437 based on a patch by Jeff King, with help from Toon Claes and Christian Couder.

Elijah Newren is a Staff Software Engineer at GitHub. He is the designer and implementer of merge-ort, Git's default merge strategy since 2.34, author of git-filter-repo—the history rewriting tool the Git project officially recommends—and a driving force behind sparse-checkout.
